title: PlantBGC: Transformer for Plant BGC Discovery via Label-Free Domain Adaptation and Weak Supervision
summary: Plant biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) encode specialized-metabolite pathways, yet curated plant BGC labels remain scarce, hindering supervised discovery at genome scale. Existing plant BGC mining tools are largely signature- and rule-driven and do not fully leverage recent advances in contextual representation learning for modeling long-range domain context and controlling false positives under strong domain shift. We seek an AI-assisted workflow that narrows experimental search space by transferring supervision from well-annotated microbial BGCs to plant genomes. We present PlantBGC, representing genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences and learning BGC-likeness with an encoder-only Transformer trained on MIBiG microbial BGCs and adapted to plants via label-free masked language modeling. On microbial benchmarks, PlantBGC achieves token-level AUC = 0.988 (10-fold CV) and 0.979 (leave-class-out). On plants, adaptation improves known-BGC recovery on n = 34 curated loci under strict 100% coverage, increasing recovery from 29.4% to 67.6% and indicating more complete boundaries. GO/KEGG-derived weak supervision reduces proxy primary-like ratio by 48.40% (GO) and 45.20% (KEGG), with consistent per-species reductions (paired Wilcoxon p = 1.53e-5). Compared to plantiSMASH, PlantBGC yields more compact loci on matched regions (median length ratio = 0.278; 93.8% of pairs are shorter).

AI.tldr: PlantBGC is an encoder-only Transformer that represents genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences, transfers supervision from microbial BGCs (MIBiG) to plant genomes via masked language modeling adaptation, and improves plant BGC recovery from 29.4% to 67.6% while producing more compact loci than plantiSMASH.
AI.motivation: Curated plant BGC labels are scarce, hindering supervised genome-scale discovery. Existing plant BGC mining tools are signature- and rule-driven and fail to leverage contextual representation learning for modeling long-range domain context or controlling false positives under strong domain shift.
AI.method: PlantBGC represents genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences and learns BGC-likeness with an encoder-only Transformer pretrained on MIBiG microbial BGCs, then adapted to plants via label-free masked language modeling. GO/KEGG-derived weak supervision is also incorporated to reduce false positives.
AI.result: PlantBGC achieves token-level AUC of 0.988 (10-fold CV) and 0.979 (leave-class-out) on microbial benchmarks. On plants, adaptation improves known-BGC recovery on 34 curated loci under strict 100% coverage from 29.4% to 67.6%. Weak supervision reduces proxy primary-like ratio by 48.40% (GO) and 45.20% (KEGG) with significant per-species reductions (paired Wilcoxon p=1.53e-5). Compared to plantiSMASH, PlantBGC yields more compact loci (median length ratio=0.278; 93.8% shorter pairs).
AI.conclusion: PlantBGC demonstrates that transferring supervision from microbial BGCs to plants via Transformer-based contextual learning is effective, yielding better recovery, more complete boundaries, fewer false positives, and more compact loci compared to existing rule-driven tools.

title: IndelFreeAligner: A Streaming Aligner for Comprehensive Gapless Alignment Against Terabase-Scale References
summary: The comparison of short sequences to massive reference databases is a cornerstone of modern genomics, but it presents a significant scalability challenge. Traditional alignment tools rely on time- and memory-intensive pre-indexing of the reference, creating a substantial bottleneck for applications involving small query sets against terabase-scale data, such as CRISPR spacer analysis. Here we present IndelFreeAligner, a streaming, indel-free alignment tool that eliminates the preprocessing bottleneck. It operates in two modes: an indexed mode for larger query sets and a brute-force mode for maximum speed on small query sets. By processing reference sequences on-the-fly, IndelFreeAligner supports user-specified mismatch thresholds up to the full query length and maintains memory usage independent of total reference size. A novel MinHitsCalculator component uses Monte Carlo simulation to determine adaptive seed-hit thresholds for indexed mode. Benchmarks against Bowtie1 and BLAST+ demonstrate that IndelFreeAligner aligns a single query against a 4 Gbp reference in 1.7 seconds versus 17 minutes for Bowtie1 (including index construction at optimal thread count), a 607-fold speedup. Against RefSeq Bacteria (560 GB compressed), IndelFreeAligner completes a 10-query search in 12 minutes using 8 GB of RAM, while BLAST+ requires 3 hours and 17 minutes to build its database alone and 506 GB of RAM to query it. Indexed mode achieves 0% false negatives through 4 substitutions (99.84-99.90% mapped at 8-16); brute-force mode is exhaustive by design. IndelFreeAligner provides a scalable and efficient solution for alignment tasks that were previously computationally prohibitive. It is distributed open-source as part of BBTools (Bushnell, 2014).

AI.tldr: IndelFreeAligner is a streaming, indel-free alignment tool that eliminates the preprocessing bottleneck of traditional aligners by processing reference sequences on-the-fly. It achieves 607x speedup over Bowtie1 for single-query alignment against 4 Gbp references and handles terabase-scale data with memory independent of reference size, using Monte Carlo simulation for adaptive seed thresholds in indexed mode.
AI.motivation: Traditional alignment tools require time- and memory-intensive pre-indexing of massive reference databases, creating a scalability bottleneck for applications with small query sets against terabase-scale data (e.g., CRISPR spacer analysis).
AI.method: IndelFreeAligner uses a streaming approach that processes reference sequences on-the-fly, eliminating preprocessing. It has two modes: brute-force mode for small query sets and indexed mode for larger sets. A novel MinHitsCalculator component uses Monte Carlo simulation to determine adaptive seed-hit thresholds for indexed mode. It supports user-specified mismatch thresholds up to full query length with memory usage independent of reference size.
AI.result: Aligns a single query against 4 Gbp reference in 1.7 seconds vs 17 minutes for Bowtie1 (607-fold speedup). Against RefSeq Bacteria (560 GB), completes 10-query search in 12 minutes using 8 GB RAM, while BLAST+ needs 3h17m just for database building and 506 GB RAM. Indexed mode achieves 0% false negatives through 4 substitutions (99.84-99.90% mapped at 8-16).
AI.conclusion: IndelFreeAligner provides a scalable and efficient solution for alignment tasks previously computationally prohibitive, distributed open-source as part of BBTools.

title: Identifying common backbones of interactions underlying food webs via non-deterministic alignments
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICASSP 2026
summary: Climate change reshapes food webs by altering species distributions and interactions, making it essential to identify structural backbones of interactions that persist across ecosystems. Deterministic alignment methods are computationally slow and restricted to one-to-one correspondences. We introduce a scalable, non-deterministic alignment framework inspired by optimal transport that captures overlapping species roles via many-to-many mappings. Framed via motif-role profiles as a Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem, our method is both efficient and interpretable. We apply the proposed method to a large continental-scale data set of 129 mammal food webs in Sub-Saharan Africa. Pairwise alignments are identified, and we uncover robust backbones with greater connectivity and transitivity than those expected under null models. The proposed approach provides a formal, reproducible tool for forecasting ecosystem reorganization and conservation efforts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a scalable, non-deterministic alignment framework based on Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport that maps species roles across food webs via many-to-many correspondences, applied to 129 Sub-Saharan African mammal food webs to uncover robust structural backbones with higher connectivity and transitivity than null models.
AI.motivation: Climate change is reshaping food webs by altering species distributions and interactions, so identifying structural backbones of interactions that persist across ecosystems is essential. Existing deterministic alignment methods are computationally slow and restricted to one-to-one correspondences, limiting their applicability to large-scale ecological analyses.
AI.method: The method frames food web alignment as a Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport problem using motif-role profiles, enabling many-to-many mappings that capture overlapping species roles across networks in an efficient, non-deterministic and interpretable manner.
AI.result: Applied to 129 mammal food webs from Sub-Saharan Africa, the method identified pairwise alignments and revealed robust backbones exhibiting greater connectivity and transitivity than expected under null models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a formal, reproducible tool for forecasting ecosystem reorganization and informing conservation efforts in the face of ongoing climate-driven changes.

title: The evolution of cooperation under imperfect phenotypic recognition
summary: Phenotypic similarity is a classical mechanism for the evolution of cooperation. Most existing models assume a binary rule in which individuals cooperate only with others of the same phenotype. This assumption is biologically restrictive, since recognition and discrimination are often gradual rather than all-or-nothing. In this paper, we extend the multidimensional phenotype-space model of cooperation by allowing the probability of helping to decline with phenotypic distance. In a large population under weak selection with mutation in both strategy and phenotype, we derive a generalized threshold for selection to favor the abundance of cooperation and express it using a new Laplace-type transform. We show that this threshold decreases strictly as discrimination becomes sharper, meaning that exact phenotype matching is the most favorable limit within this family of recognition rules. We also show that the threshold decreases strictly with phenotype-space dimension, meaning that higher-dimensional phenotype spaces promote cooperation even when recognition is imperfect. Our asymptotic analysis further shows that low phenotype mutations strongly inhibit cooperation, whereas sufficiently high phenotype mutations drive the threshold toward its minimal value. However, high strategy mutation makes cooperation harder to maintain.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the multidimensional phenotype-space model of cooperation by replacing binary phenotype matching with gradual discrimination, where helping probability declines continuously with phenotypic distance. The authors derive a generalized selection threshold using a Laplace-type transform and show that sharper discrimination, higher phenotype-space dimensionality, and high phenotype mutation promote cooperation, while high strategy mutation hinders it.
AI.motivation: Existing models of phenotype-based cooperation assume a binary rule (cooperate only with identical phenotypes), which is biologically unrealistic since recognition and discrimination in nature are typically gradual rather than all-or-nothing. This motivates extending the model to continuous recognition rules.
AI.method: The authors extend the multidimensional phenotype-space model by allowing the probability of helping to decline with phenotypic distance. They analyze a large population under weak selection with mutation in both strategy and phenotype, and derive a generalized threshold for cooperation to be favored using a new Laplace-type transform.
AI.result: The cooperation threshold decreases strictly as discrimination becomes sharper (exact matching is most favorable), decreases strictly with phenotype-space dimension, is strongly inhibited by low phenotype mutation while sufficiently high phenotype mutations drive the threshold toward its minimal value, and high strategy mutation makes cooperation harder to maintain.
AI.conclusion: Gradual phenotype discrimination still supports cooperation, but sharper recognition is more favorable. Higher-dimensional phenotype spaces promote cooperation even under imperfect recognition, while the mutation dynamics differentially affect the viability of cooperation through strategy and phenotype channels.

title: Evolutionary adaptation through bet-hedging in finite populations under fluctuating environments
summary: Natural populations evolve under fluctuating environments and limited resources, yet it is unclear how these factors jointly shape adaptation. Here, we introduce a minimal stochastic model of a population undergoing a birth-death process in a randomly switching environment, where individuals inherit phenotypic strategies that determine the distribution of phenotypes across generations. First, we confirm that environmental variability can favor phenotypic diversity (bet-hedging), and that the strategy maximizing the average growth rate generally differs from the one minimizing extinction risk. We then demonstrate that evolution drives populations toward strategies that balance these competing objectives. Furthermore, we show that population size modulates this evolutionary outcome: large populations converge to the growth-maximizing strategy, whereas smaller ones evolve toward more resilient strategies. Finally, we provide a simple heuristic approximation that captures these results, clarifying the interplay between growth, extinction, and mutation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a minimal stochastic birth-death model of populations in randomly switching environments to investigate how environmental variability and population size jointly shape adaptation. The authors show that evolution balances growth maximization against extinction risk minimization, with large populations converging to growth-optimal strategies while smaller populations favor more resilient (bet-hedging) strategies, and provide a heuristic approximation capturing these dynamics.
AI.motivation: Natural populations evolve under fluctuating environments and limited resources, but it remains unclear how environmental variability and resource constraints jointly shape adaptation. This gap motivates a need for a tractable theoretical framework to understand the interplay between these factors in evolutionary dynamics.
AI.method: The authors construct a minimal stochastic model of a population undergoing a birth-death process in a randomly switching environment. Individuals inherit phenotypic strategies that determine phenotype distributions across generations, allowing analysis of how environmental variability, population size, mutation, and extinction risk interact in shaping evolutionary outcomes.
AI.result: Environmental variability favors phenotypic diversity (bet-hedging). The strategy maximizing average growth rate generally differs from that minimizing extinction risk. Evolution drives populations toward strategies balancing these competing objectives, with population size as a key modulator: large populations converge to growth-maximizing strategies while smaller populations evolve toward more resilient strategies. A simple heuristic approximation captures these results.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between growth, extinction, and mutation is clarified through a single minimal model, demonstrating that population size critically determines whether evolution prioritizes growth maximization or resilience (extinction avoidance), with the heuristic approximation providing insights into these competing evolutionary pressures.

title: A data-driven stage-structured host-parasitoid model for optimizing Trichogramma interventions against soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) outbreaks
summary: The soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) poses a severe threat to global soybean production.In this study, we developed a stage-structured host-parasitoid dynamic model that explicitly couples the holometabolous life cycle of the pest with the obligate egg-parasitism mechanism of Trichogramma wasps. Utilizing field monitoring data from Changchun, Jilin Province, key biological parameters were rigorously estimated via the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method.This calibration facilitated the establishment of a precise Economic Injury Level ($Q_{EIL}$) of 0.0389 individuals/$m^2$, based solely on the destructive larval stage. Through theoretical and numerical analyses of different intervention scenarios, we identified an optimal continuous release rate ($C^* = 2.645$) that efficiently suppresses the outbreak without causing wasteful parasitoid accumulation. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that a 5-day impulsive release interval provides the optimal balance between strict pest suppression and field operational costs. This study bridges the gap between theoretical population dynamics and applied agricultural management, providing a directly applicable mathematical decision-making tool for the precise biological control of crop pests.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a stage-structured host-parasitoid model coupling the soybean pod borer's life cycle with Trichogramma wasp egg parasitism, calibrated via MCMC using field data to establish an Economic Injury Level and identify optimal release strategies for biological control.
AI.motivation: The soybean pod borer poses a severe threat to global soybean production, and there is a need for mathematically grounded, precise biological control strategies to manage this pest effectively.
AI.method: A stage-structured host-parasitoid dynamic model is constructed that couples the pest's holometabolous life cycle with the obligate egg-parasitism of Trichogramma wasps. Parameters are estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with field data from Changchun, Jilin Province. Theoretical and numerical analyses of intervention scenarios are used to determine optimal release rates and intervals.
AI.result: An Economic Injury Level (Q_EIL) of 0.0389 individuals/m² was established based on the destructive larval stage. An optimal continuous release rate (C* = 2.645) was identified that suppresses outbreaks without wasteful parasitoid accumulation, and a 5-day impulsive release interval was found to balance pest suppression and operational costs.
AI.conclusion: The study bridges theoretical population dynamics and applied agricultural management, providing a directly applicable mathematical decision-making tool for precise biological control of crop pests.

title: Stimulus-Evoked Network Dynamics in Human Cortical Organoids: From a Graph-Computational Framework to Repeated-Stimulation Depression
summary: Human cortical organoids provide an experimentally accessible model of early neural circuit formation, yet whether their activity reflects structured information processing rather than spontaneous synchronization is unclear. We developed a graph-computational framework to quantify stimulus-evoked propagation. This includes stimulus-conditioned functional graphs, a graph-constrained dynamical (graph-neural-network) model used as a system-identification tool, a biological message-passing principle bounding integration depth by observable propagation depth, and a suite of graph-level metrics. We carried this program out in full on longitudinal HD-MEA recordings from three organoids. Once the true acquisition sampling rate and stimulus timing were recovered, the evoked response proved to be a fast, near-synchronous network burst with no measurable outward propagation (peak-latency vs. distance slope = 0). The propagation/integration-depth metrics (Deff ,reachability index, dmax) therefore do not apply, and per-day connectivity graphs were not reliably estimable at the available trial count, a negative result with methodological consequences for applying such metrics to organoid data. Reframing around synchrony, response-population size and shared variability revealed a control-validated phenomenon, i.e., repeated daily stimulation progressively depressed and spatially contracted the evoked response. That repeated stimulation reshapes organoid networks is established, but longitudinal designs in which every preparation is stimulated cannot separate this from developmental maturation. We break that confound with a developmentally-matched, stimulation-naive control, where at day 7, an organoid receiving its first-ever stimulation engaged 93% of the array, whereas organoids with five prior sessions engaged 10%.

AI.tldr: The authors developed a graph-computational framework to analyze stimulus-evoked activity in cortical organoids, but found no measurable spatial propagation — responses were fast, near-synchronous network bursts. Reframing around synchrony, they revealed that repeated daily stimulation progressively depresses and spatially contracts the evoked response, validated with a stimulation-naive control showing first-stimulation organoids engage 93% of the array vs. 10% for previously stimulated ones.
AI.motivation: To determine whether activity in human cortical organoids reflects structured information processing (e.g., stimulus-evoked propagation) rather than mere spontaneous synchronization, and to build a rigorous quantitative framework to test this.
AI.method: A graph-computational framework including stimulus-conditioned functional graphs, a graph-neural-network dynamical model for system identification, a biological message-passing principle, and graph-level metrics. Applied to longitudinal HD-MEA recordings from three organoids, with recovered sampling rates and stimulus timing, plus a developmentally-matched stimulation-naive control to break the repeated-stimulation confound.
AI.result: Evoked responses were fast, near-synchronous network bursts with no outward propagation (peak-latency vs. distance slope = 0), so propagation metrics did not apply and connectivity graphs were not reliably estimable. Reframing around synchrony revealed that repeated daily stimulation progressively depressed and spatially contracted responses: a first-stimulation organoid engaged 93% of the array vs. 10% for organoids with five prior sessions.
AI.conclusion: Repeated stimulation itself reshapes organoid networks (depressing and contracting their responses), and longitudinal designs that stimulate every preparation confound this effect with developmental maturation. The study provides methodological caution for applying propagation-based metrics to organoid data and demonstrates the need for naive controls.

title: Hash Chemistry: Minimal Models for Evolutionary Growth of Complexity
summary: Hash Chemistry is a family of minimalistic evolutionary models in which a deterministic hash function assigns a scalar score to entities of arbitrary size, opening a combinatorially vast possibility space (a ``cardinality leap''). Since its introduction, the idea has been realized in several settings, from the original spatial formulation to a fast non-spatial variant and then to structural cellular models. Here we review the Hash Chemistry family as a coherent modeling framework and use it to explore how minimal systems can demonstrate the mechanisms behind multiscale open-ended evolutionary dynamics. The most recent model, Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC), successfully demonstrated multiscale ecological interaction/adaptation and complexity growth of replicators in a computationally efficient manner. In this study, we first extend SCHC to incorporate spatial locality and dyadicity of competitive interactions among replicating structures. We show this extension substantially enhances SCHC's evolutionary dynamics. Furthermore, we explore SCHC in a significantly larger spatial domain using a GPU-accelerated implementation. We show that the size of the space acts as a control parameter for a stochastic, nucleation-like transition between a compact-replicator regime and a runaway size-dominance regime, and we separate the responsible mechanism into a non-spatial, size-biased sampling feedback and a finite-size spatial effect. Altogether, these results illustrate the rich potential of Hash Chemistry as a minimal, mechanistically transparent testbed for studying open-ended evolution across scales.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the Hash Chemistry family of minimalistic evolutionary models and extends Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC) with spatial locality and dyadicity of competitive interactions, then explores it in a large GPU-accelerated spatial domain, revealing a stochastic nucleation-like transition between compact-replicator and runaway size-dominance regimes driven by size-biased sampling feedback and finite-size spatial effects.
AI.motivation: To establish Hash Chemistry as a coherent modeling framework for studying multiscale open-ended evolutionary dynamics, and to further enhance and understand the mechanisms—particularly spatial effects and scaling—behind the existing SCHC model's success in demonstrating multiscale ecological interaction and complexity growth.
AI.method: The authors extend Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC) to incorporate spatial locality and dyadicity (pairwise) of competitive interactions among replicating structures. They implement the model on a GPU-accelerated platform to explore substantially larger spatial domains and analyze the resulting evolutionary dynamics.
AI.result: The spatial and dyadic extension substantially enhances SCHC's evolutionary dynamics. In large spatial domains, the space size acts as a control parameter for a stochastic, nucleation-like transition between a compact-replicator regime and a runaway size-dominance regime. The responsible mechanism is separated into a non-spatial, size-biased sampling feedback and a finite-size spatial effect.
AI.conclusion: These results illustrate the rich potential of Hash Chemistry as a minimal, mechanistically transparent testbed for studying open-ended evolution across scales.

title: Causal Architecture Dynamics Prior to Arrival of Self-replicators in a Model of Catalytic Networks Relevant to Origin-of-Life
summary: Agents that exert causal power in the world are thought to be the product of selection among diverse replicators; what is the causal structure of a medium before replicators appear, and evolution takes hold? We studied information-theoretic dynamics of the popular GARD model that captures several dynamics thought to be important at life's origin and found that causal emergence predicted the initial appearance of self-replication. Moreover, interventions that drove causal emergence up increased the longevity of self-replicators, while interventions that drove causal emergence down decreased the abundance of these self-replicators, suggesting causal emergence as a functional control knob. Thus, progressive increases in integrated causality are detectable in active media before evolutionary dynamics begin to operate, which may have implications for the origin of life across highly diverse scenarios and for understanding the forces driving the rise in causal power observed in the biosphere on Earth.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the information-theoretic dynamics of the GARD model (a prebiotic self-replication model) and finds that causal emergence—a measure of integrated causality—predicts the initial appearance of self-replication before evolution takes hold. Manipulating causal emergence up or down correspondingly increases or decreases the longevity and abundance of self-replicators, positioning it as a functional control knob in prebiotic systems.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to understand what causal structure exists in a medium before Darwinian selection and replication appear—i.e., what forces drive the rise of causal power in agents before evolution begins operating.
AI.method: The authors analyze information-theoretic dynamics of the GARD (Graded Autocatalysis Replication Domain) model, which captures behaviors relevant to life's origin. They measure causal emergence and test how interventions that increase or decrease it affect the appearance, longevity, and abundance of self-replicators.
AI.result: Causal emergence predicts the initial appearance of self-replication. Upscaling causal emergence increases self-replicator longevity; downscaling it decreases their abundance, demonstrating a causal, tunable relationship.
AI.conclusion: Progressive increases in integrated causality are detectable in active media even before evolutionary dynamics start, suggesting causal emergence may be a universal driver relevant to the origin of life across diverse scenarios and to understanding rising causal power in Earth's biosphere.

title: Multi-scale measures of time-varying epidemic spread on human mobility networks
summary: Human movement drives the spatial spread and persistence of many infectious diseases, yet existing theory and real-time operational tools for inferring the instantaneous reproduction number R(t) often assume static and/or homogeneously mixing populations and cannot describe how individuals generate and acquire infections heterogeneously based on their movement patterns within a day. Renewal equations underpin many such popular estimators of R(t), and here, we develop a network-based modelling framework from which we derive new mechanism-led renewal equations and control indicators for outbreaks of infectious diseases. These equations directly integrate within-day human movement to rigorously define a family of instantaneous reproduction numbers; inward, outward, and type R(t) for individual locations, R(t) between locations, R(t) at meeting locations, and R(t) for the entire mobility network. These quantities correct for the unsuitability of existing location-specific R(t) estimators that operate in closed, static populations. Applying our framework to epidemics on diverse types of networks alongside mobile phone data, we demonstrate how our new framework's outputs provide new, multi-scale control indicators at the network, location, and transmission corridor scales, and can be used to design targeted disease control interventions including the strength, type, and length of intervention required across space and time. We capture the biasing effects of different existing ways to measure location-specific and network-level transmission potential without capturing within-day human movements. This generalisable framework redefines reproduction numbers in real-world outbreaks that are shaped by individuals moving across connected locations, enabling more spatially and temporally precise interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a network-based modeling framework with new mechanism-led renewal equations that directly integrate within-day human movement to define a family of instantaneous reproduction numbers (inward, outward, type, between-location, meeting-location, and network-level R(t)), correcting for biases in existing location-specific estimators that assume static, homogeneously mixing populations.
AI.motivation: Existing R(t) estimation tools assume static and/or homogeneously mixing populations, failing to capture how individuals generate and acquire infections heterogeneously based on their within-day movement patterns. This limits the spatial and temporal precision of outbreak control.
AI.method: The authors derive new mechanism-led renewal equations from a network-based modeling framework that explicitly integrates within-day human movement patterns, defining a hierarchy of instantaneous reproduction numbers across different spatial scales (locations, between locations, meeting locations, and the whole mobility network), validated on diverse network types and mobile phone data.
AI.result: The framework provides multi-scale control indicators at network, location, and transmission corridor scales, enables design of targeted interventions (strength, type, length), quantifies biasing effects of existing location-specific and network-level R(t) estimators that ignore within-day movement, and demonstrates improved spatiotemporal precision for interventions.
AI.conclusion: This generalizable framework redefines reproduction numbers for real-world outbreaks shaped by human movement across connected locations, enabling more spatially and temporally precise disease control interventions.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that provides flexible EEG signal reconstruction, supporting variable-length sequences up to 30s, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial temporal interval reconstruction, performing on par with its predecessor ZUNA1 while being far more flexible and outperforming standard methods like spherical spline interpolation.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG reconstruction methods (e.g., spherical spline interpolation) are rigid and limited in their capabilities. There is a need for a flexible reconstruction model that can handle variable sequence lengths, arbitrary numbers of channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and partial temporal coverage within channels.
AI.method: A 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder that extends the earlier ZUNA1 model with enhanced flexibility, capable of reconstructing EEG signals of variable length (up to 30s), with arbitrary channel counts/positions, and arbitrary temporal intervals within channels, in addition to full-channel reconstruction.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with ZUNA1 while being significantly more flexible across a wide range of reconstruction tasks. It continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction baselines such as spherical spline interpolation.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 offers a flexible, high-performance EEG reconstruction solution that matches its predecessor's quality while supporting a much broader range of reconstruction scenarios, and is released open source under Apache 2.0.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
summary: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Rational Mentalizing model explaining how people decide between social and non-social learning by estimating the utility of observing others (via theory of mind) and weighing it against direct exploration, validated with a novel game showing quantitative fit to human behavior.
AI.motivation: Although social learning is powerful, humans often choose direct experience over it despite potential costs. The authors aim to understand how people balance social versus non-social learning strategies.
AI.method: A Rational Mentalizing model is proposed that reasons about another agent's goals and the informativeness of their future actions to estimate the utility of social learning, then compares this against the utility of non-social learning. A novel game was designed where players choose between observing others or exploring the environment to test the model.
AI.result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social and non-social learning strategies in the novel game.
AI.conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind in the service of utility maximization.

title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
summary: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

AI.tldr: KAISEN is a five-phase clinical risk model audit pipeline (subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, drift monitoring) stress-tested to failure on synthetic benchmarks. Key findings: significance tracks each axis's minimum detectable effect; threshold optimization reliably reduces equalized-odds disparity while calibration does not; mechanism diagnostics fail silently under proxy misspecification; and drift monitoring thresholds do not transfer across cohorts.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk models show strong aggregate performance but heterogeneous error rates across patient subgroups. Existing audit pipelines are rarely stress-tested, leaving unclear which components are trustworthy and under what conditions.
AI.method: Builds KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline, and evaluates it to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections with known ground truth.
AI.result: (i) Rank correlation between significance count and raw EOD is rho=0.56, rising to rho=0.78 after standardizing by minimum detectable effect. (ii) Threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48/48 held-out runs (delta=-0.285, 95% CI [-0.313,-0.252]) while Platt scaling behaves as a coin flip (19/48 improved). (iii) Mechanism diagnostic classifies 144/144 controlled cases correctly but recovers 0/48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification with no failure signal. (iv) CUSUM false alarms and missed shifts track cohort realization over disease (chi-squared p=0.002).
AI.conclusion: Audit pipelines have failure modes that are silent and systematic; what an audit should report is variance rather than averages, and thresholds tuned on one cohort do not transfer. Results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity.
